sections.title: 讲座 1
sections.transcript: We've been talking about the law of inertia. An object moving in a straight line will continue to move in a straight line unless it is acted upon by another force. So what does this mean in the real world? Let's look at something many people do all the time, riding a bicycle. Think about riding along in a straight line. Once the bike is moving, inertia will keep it going in a straight line. But we don't just ride in straight lines, do we? We turn at corners and steer around things that are in our way. So how do you get the bicycle not to go straight? Easy, right? Don't you just need to turn the front wheel in the direction you want to turn? In fact, if you only turn the front wheel, you're likely to end up on the pavement. The wheel will turn, but because of inertia, your body and the rest of the bike will want to keep moving straight ahead. So how does a cyclist avoid this? The key is to lean in. Weight needs to shift in the direction of the turn so that the force of gravity can work against the force of inertia. Professional cyclists who move at high speeds need to hit a sweet spot. They must lean more to keep their bicycles from sliding out of turns, but not too much. At a certain point, gravity will bring both rider and bicycle down to the ground.

sections.transcript: Multispecies anthropology flips that perspective. It sees humans and other species, animals, plants, even fungi as Co participants in shared worlds. Instead of reducing non humans to cultural symbols, it highlights their agency, their ability to act, adapt and influence human lives. Take the studies of mushroom foraging in Siberia. Here fungi, trees and humans form interdependent networks. The growth of matsutake mushrooms depends on and reflects forest Health and Human harvesting practices, even as harvesting practices and forest health are influenced by the mushrooms themselves. The point is, life isn't a human story with animals or plants in the background. It's a web of relationships among many kinds of beings. Next, I'll explore how this multispecies perspective reshapes research methods, what it means to study not just human cultures, but the entangled lives of humans and other beings.

sections.title: 讲座 1
sections.transcript: Picture a creature that's smaller than a mouse, yet as territorial as a lion. Does it sound like a cartoon character? It's actually the real life Scarlet badis, A freshwater fish. It's only about 2 cm long at most. In the wild, it generally thrives peacefully in the slow moving streams of India. Because of its size and attractive coloring, it's also a popular choice for aquariums and fish tanks. However, in captive environments like aquariums, males are more aggressive. They'll chase and nip at other males if they encroach on their territory, so it's crucial to include lots of vegetation. Plants act as hiding places and borderlines between males territories. Now, male Scarlet badis are a vivid orangish red scarlet with light bluish stripes. When a male isn't having a confrontation with another male in the aquarium, though, his scarlet is less bright. It can almost but not quite resemble female coloring, which is dull gray. This could make it hard to tell the sexes apart, except if you can see any scarlet at all on the fish, it's a male. Plus, unlike in most fish species, males are also usually a bit larger than females. And the other time a male Scarlet basis shows his brightest coloring is during breeding season in aquariums, he can be observed doing a sort of dance to impress females, showing himself off. His dance also involves following the female around until she decides whether to mate with him.

sections.title: 讲座 1
sections.transcript: Today we're going to talk about the importance of sleep for cognitive function. Sleep is crucial for maintaining various aspects of brain health. One of the key benefits of sleep is the consolidation of memory. During sleep, particularly during the deep sleep stages, the brain processes and stores information acquired during the day, making it easier to recall later. During deep sleep, the brain also undergoes a process that flushes out neurotoxins like beta amyloid, which are linked to Alzheimer's disease. Sleep helps in learning new skills and knowledge by strengthening neural connections, and it allows the brain to enhance problem solving abilities by reorganizing information. Studies have shown that sleep deprivation affects cognitive functions like attention and decision making. Another critical aspect of sleep is its role in emotional regulation. During sleep, the brain can process emotional experiences, which helps maintain emotional stability. REM sleep in particular plays a key role in recalibrating the brain's emotional circuits, helping people better manage fear and anxiety responses. People who do not get enough sleep are more likely to experience mood swings, anxiety, and depression. Despite the clear benefits of sleep, many people still struggle with getting enough rest. It's essential to prioritize sleep and adopt good sleep hygiene practices such as maintaining a regular sleep schedule, avoiding caffeine and electronic screens before bedtime, and creating a comfortable sleep environment. By doing so, individuals can improve their cognitive function and overall well being.

sections.title: 讲座 2
sections.transcript: Positive reinforcement is a powerful concept in psychology and behavior training. It means giving a reward after someone performs an action you want them to do again. The basic idea is that when a behavior leads to a positive outcome, it's more likely to be repeated. In other words, we tend to repeat actions that bring us something positive. This principle applies to both humans and animals, but the way it works can differ. Animals need to receive rewards immediately after the desired behavior. For example, if a dog sits and gets a treat right away, it learns that sitting leads to something good. If the reward comes too late, the connection is lost. Humans, however, can understand delayed rewards. They might work hard today because they're aiming for a future goal, like earning a degree. Or they might feel motivated by praise even if the reward isn't tangible or instant. But rewards must be used carefully. If a parent gives a child candy to stop whining, the child may learn that whining gets rewarded. It's like watering weeds instead of flowers. You're encouraging the wrong behavior. And if rewards are given too frequently, they can reduce a person's internal motivation, making them rely more on external incentives to take action. So while positive reinforcement is effective, it works best when applied thoughtfully and with clear intent.

sections.transcript: The Renaissance was a pivotal period in European history. Spanning roughly the 14th to the 17th centuries, the Renaissance is characterized by a renewed interest in art, science and literature. It marked a significant departure from the Middle Ages and laid the groundwork for the modern era. One of the defining features of the Renaissance was the revival of classical learning. Scholars and artists looked back to the texts and artistic achievements of ancient Greece and Rome for inspiration. This led to a flourishing of ideas and creativity evident in the works of figures like Leonardo da Vinci, Michelangelo and Galileo Galilei. The invention of the printing press by Johannes Gutenberg around 1440 was a crucial development during this time. It allowed for the mass production of books, making literature and scholarly works more accessible to a broader audience. This contributed to increased literacy and the spread of Renaissance ideas. The Renaissance also saw major advancements in science, particularly in astronomy. Nicolaus Copernicus proposed a heliocentric model of the solar system, placing the sun, not the Earth, as the center. Galileo Galilei later used a telescope to observe celestial bodies, providing evidence that supported Copernicus theory. These discoveries challenged long held beliefs and laid the foundation for modern astronomy. Despite political instability in some regions, the Renaissance left a lasting legacy on European society. Its influence can still be seen today in art, science and education.

sections.title: 讲座 2
sections.transcript: Urbanization is frequently associated with negative outcomes. Pollution, overcrowding and especially traffic congestion. In many cities, poor planning has led to increased noise and emissions as well as reduced quality of life. However, urbanization doesn't have to be this way if approached thoughtfully. An alternative to traffic jams and congested city streets is to foster sustainable transportation. Copenhagen in Denmark, for instance, has made bicycles a central part of its urban design. The city's extensive network of protected bike lanes and pro cycling policies have encouraged residents to choose bicycles over cars. In addition to lowering automobile emissions, this shift has also improved public health and reduced traffic related stress. Also, when kept in control and planned properly, urbanization, in this case, compact urban living, minimizes land use and energy consumption compared to sprawling suburban development. Suburban neighborhoods require large plots of land for individual homes, roads and parking. When housing, services and infrastructure are concentrated, this can actually preserve surrounding natural areas and agricultural lands. So, even though this may seem strange, urban growth is actually more compatible with environmental conservation. Urbanization also, by necessity, has led to some innovative thinking, especially concerning the efficient use of land and space. Many cities are incorporating such innovation in food production by creating rooftop farms and using vertical agriculture, which grows crops in stacked vertical layers. In particular, Singapore has invested in high tech urban farming systems that grow vegetables in controlled environments, helping increase local food supply and reduce dependence on imports.

sections.title: 讲座 2
sections.transcript: This is called inattentional blindness, a phenomenon where concentrating on one thing can make us overlook something happening right in front of us. A classic study illustrates this perfectly. Participants watched a video of people passing a basketball and were asked to count passes made by players in white shirts. Midway through the video, a person in a gorilla suit walked into the scene, thumped its chest and left. Astonishingly, about half the viewers never saw the gorilla. Their attention was locked on counting passes. In real world situations, inattentional blindness can have serious consequences. For example, while driving, focusing on finding a street sign might make you miss a pedestrian stepping into the road. Recognizing this tendency can help us stay safer and more aware. Interestingly, psychologists trace this phenomenon to a useful ability, selective attention. This is the brain's way of filtering sensory input to avoid overload, allowing us to concentrate on important tasks. Think about sitting in a noisy open plan office writing a report. Phones are ringing, people are talking, but you managed to tune it all out and focus on your work. That's selective attention at its best.

sections.title: 讲座 2
sections.transcript: For example, researchers have utilized bioacoustics to monitor whale populations. By recording and analyzing whale songs, scientists can track their movements and estimate population sizes. This information is vital for creating effective conservation strategies. Similarly, studying bird songs helps ornithologists understand mating rituals in territory establishment. These acoustic signals are often complex and specific to each species, providing a wealth of information about their social structures. Insects, too, use sounds for communication, particularly during mating. The chirping of crickets and buzzing of bees are examples of how bioacoustics plays a role in their life cycles. Despite its benefits, bioacoustics research faces challenges. The equipment needed for recording and analyzing sounds can be expensive and requires specialized knowledge to operate. Additionally, environmental noise such as traffic, machinery or even wind can interfere with the clarity of recordings, making it difficult to study certain species. Nonetheless, advancements in technology continue to improve the capabilities of bioacoustics, making it an invaluable tool for studying and protecting wildlife.

sections.title: 讲座 1
sections.transcript: • 0:00 / 1:32 : Listen to a lecture in a music class. If you're familiar with ancient Greece, you know how important music was in everyday life. You can probably imagine people sitting in a Greek amphitheater, completely absorbed by the sounds filling the air. But music wasn't only heard in theater performances. It played a role in all kinds of settings, including religious ceremonies and athletic competitions. One instrument that stands out is the aulos. This aulos is a double reeded wind instrument that was a big part of Greek musical life, and it has a distinctive design. It has two pipes, each with a reed, usually made from a plant, similar to what you'd find in a modern oboe. And because the pipes are cylindrical, not conical like some other wind instruments, it produces a sound that's rich and sharp. That unique sound helped bring out emotion in plays and public events, which brought depth to the drama unfolding on stage. To really master the aulos, the player had to be highly skilled. One technique they used was circular breathing. It means inhaling air through the nose while simultaneously pushing air out through the cheeks. This allowed them to play long, continuous passages without stopping for breath. Even though the aulos was hugely important in ancient times, it eventually faded from use as other instruments and musical styles took over. Still, its legacy lives on as it gives us a glimpse into the musical world of ancient Greece.

sections.title: 讲座 2
sections.transcript: Have you ever been so engrossed in a task that you completely missed something obvious? This is called inattentional blindness, a phenomenon where concentrating on one thing can make us overlook something happening right in front of us. A classic study illustrates this perfectly. Participants watched a video of people passing a basketball and were asked to count passes made by players in white shirts. Midway through the video, a person in a gorilla suit walked into the scene, thumped its chest and left. Astonishingly, about half the viewers never saw the gorilla. Their attention was locked on counting passes. In real world situations, inattentional blindness can have serious consequences. For example, while driving, focusing on finding a street sign might make you miss a pedestrian stepping into the road. Recognizing this tendency can help us stay safer and more aware. Interestingly, psychologists trace this phenomenon to a useful ability, selective attention. This is the brains way of filtering sensory input to avoid overload, allowing us to concentrate on important tasks. Think about sitting in a noisy open plan office writing a report. Phones are ringing, people are talking, but you managed to tune it all out and focus on your work. That's selective attention at its best.

sections.transcript: Basically, the correct choice was totally obvious. Each person announced aloud which line matched the standard, and those who were in on the study deliberately gave the wrong answer first. The real participant answered last. Across 12 trials, 75% of participants conformed with the incorrect answers that people in the group had given before them at least once, so they chose the line that was clearly wrong. This indicates strong influence of group pressure. This study was replicated in 1980, roughly 30 years after Ashe conducted his experiment. The subjects in this experiment were British university students. Interestingly, conformity was much lower with these participants. This suggests that conformity may be influenced by culture and the country people grow up in.

sections.title: 讲座 1
sections.transcript: Listen to a podcast about political science. Listen to a podcast about political science. Soft power refers to a country's ability to influence others through attraction, culture, and collaboration. The term was introduced by political scientist Joseph Nye in 1990. He noticed that some countries gain support not by using force or money, but by being admired and respected. What Nye contributed wasn't just a name. He offered a clear framework for understanding this kind of influence. He explained that power works in three ways: by forcing others, by paying them, or by attracting them. That third kind, attraction, is what he called soft power. By classifying power this way, he made it easier for people to understand and talk about influence that comes from trust, culture, and values. A modern example is South Korea's cultural wave, which has sparked global interest in Korean pop music, language, and food. This kind of appeal fits directly into Nye's idea of attraction. It shows how cultural influence can build admiration and shape international relationships without pressure or incentives. Now, soft power takes time because it's built on trust, reputation, and emotional connection. It spreads through cultural events, learning opportunities, and other shared experiences, things that grow gradually but once established, it tends to last, often shaping how future generations view a country. Like planting a tree, it needs patience and care, but its roots run deep and its impact endures.

sections.title: 讲座 1
sections.transcript: 0:00 / 2:16 : Expressionist artists aim to convey their inner feelings and perceptions through distorted and exaggerated forms, vivid colors, and bold brushstrokes. One of the most famous Expressionist artists is Edvard Munch. His painting The Scream shows an agonized person crying out. It eventually became an icon of the movement's focus on intense personal experience. Expressionism was not limited to visual arts, however. It also influenced literary, theater and cinematic arts. In literature, authors like Franz Kafka explored themes of alienation and existential angst in his bizarre, dreamlike fiction. Expressionist theater often used dramatic lighting and intense performances to evoke emotional responses. Set sometimes featured oversized symbolic objects. In Elmer Rice's 1923 play The Adding Machine, a giant adding machine represents the dehumanizing forces of technology. Similarly, the German Expressionist film movement used innovative techniques, such as cutting between scenes with a shared sound to help create emotionally charged narratives. Despite its impact, Expressionism faced criticism for its departure from traditional aesthetics and its emphasis on the personal. Critics argued that its focus on subjective emotion robbed the works of broader content or meaning. And the bold brushwork in painting was sometimes viewed as lacking in skill and technique. Nonetheless, Expressionism paved the way for later movements such as Surrealism, leaving a lasting legacy in the art world.

sections.transcript: Another notable example is The Catcher in the Rye by J.D.Salinger. The protagonist, Holden Caulfield, feels disconnected from the world around him, and he struggles with alienation and loneliness. This social isolation is what drives Holden's actions and internal conflicts throughout the book. Yet another example of isolation in literature, and one that ends badly, is Herman Melville's Moby Dick. In this novel, Captain Ahab's obsessive, vengeful quest for the white whale leads to his isolation. This obsession distances him from his crew as well as his humanity, and it propels him and his ship toward a destructive end. However, the portrayal of isolation in literature is not always negative. In Charlotte Bronte's Jane Eyre, the titular character experiences isolation at various points in her life, such as when she is sent to live with her unkind relatives and later when she experiences loneliness at a boarding school. But Jane is resilient in the face of isolation, becoming strong and independent.

sections.title: 讲座 1
sections.transcript: Listen to part of a psychology podcast. My brother Alex has always wanted to get a cat. He likes cats better than dogs. One day he sent me an online article titled Which Pet is Right for You and says see, even experts agree cats are better. But when I read the article, nowhere did it say that. The article presents balanced facts. Dogs are loyal and trainable while cats are independent and low maintenance. My brother was not being dishonest, he simply focused only on the parts that favor cats and skimmed over or dismissed the parts that highlight dogs' advantages. This is called confirmation bias. Our brains are lazy. They like consistency. Information that aligns with what we already know is easier to understand and less mentally taxing. So our brains seek it out and filter out the rest. This affects the decisions we make in our daily life as well as in work. Scientists are not immune to confirmation bias. Researchers may unintentionally design experiments or interpret data in ways that support their hypotheses, overlooking results that do not fit their expectations. Flawed conclusions in scientific studies can lead to serious consequences. So what can we do to minimize confirmation bias? The first step is to recognize the existence of confirmation bias. Know that you might be biased. Then actively seek out information that challenges your beliefs. Don't only talk with people who hold the same views as yours and slow down. Don't make hasty decisions.

sections.title: 讲座 2
sections.transcript: Have you ever wondered why certain songs evoke strong emotions or memories? This phenomenon is rooted in the field of music psychology, which examines how music impacts our feelings, thoughts, and behaviors. Research indicates that music can trigger a range of emotional responses through its rhythm, melody, and lyrics. For example, upbeat songs often make us feel happy and energetic. On the other hand, slow, melancholic tunes can evoke sadness or nostalgia. But why does this happen? One theory suggests that music stimulates the brain's reward system. That is, it releases a chemical called dopamine. Dopamine is a neurotransmitter associated with pleasure and motivation. In addition, music is often intertwined with personal experiences. Hearing a song that played during a significant life event can bring back vivid memories and the emotions associated with them. I should point out, though, the individual responses to music can vary greatly. Idiosyncratic factors that play a role in how we perceive and react to different types of music include cultural background, personality, and the context in which we hear the song. Now, this effect that music has on emotional well-being is the basis for music therapy, which has been useful in treating a variety of psychological conditions like stress or anxiety. By leveraging music's emotional power, music therapists can help patients reduce stress and improve their overall well-being. More research is needed, but our growing understanding of music psychology points to its even greater benefits for mental health and emotional regulation in the future.

sections.title: 讲座 1
sections.transcript: Previously, we discussed the significance of pottery to ancient cultures, including pottery as an art form and pottery's crucial role in trade. Today, we'll focus on the development of pottery over time. 1 breakthrough was the invention of the Potter's wheel around 3500 BCE in Mesopotamia. Before this, pottery was shaped mostly by hand, which was slow and produced less uniform results. The Potter's wheel allowed artisans to spin and shape the clay more quickly and evenly, making it possible to create symmetrical vessels with greater precision and speed. Firing technology also advanced. Early pots were fired in open pits, which limited temperature control, resulting in uneven or fragile pots. So kilns were developed: enclosed ovens that could reach higher and more consistent temperatures. These allowed for stronger, more durable pottery. Another advance was the updraft kiln, which directed heat upward through the chamber. By adjusting the airflow, Potters could control how much oxygen reached the fire. This helped them produce pottery with specific colors, like red or black, depending on how the clay reacted to the firing atmosphere. Then, in ancient China, Potters developed kilns that could reach very high temperatures. This allowed them to create stoneware and eventually porcelain. Porcelain is made from a special mix of fine clay and minerals and must be fired at temperatures above 1200°C. The result is a smooth white ceramic that is strong, lightweight, and slightly translucent. Porcelain was a major breakthrough because it was more durable and versatile than earlier pottery.

sections.title: 讲座 2
sections.transcript: Let's discuss the role of startup incubators in supporting new businesses. These are programs designed to help startups navigate the early stages of development and increase their chances of success by providing resources, mentorship, and networking. What resources might a new business lack? Incubators often provide office space and equipment to help start-ups get off the ground, and they also steer new businesses toward funding opportunities. Many new entrepreneurs will lack the financial means to invest in basic necessities themselves, and this support can be invaluable. Another important element of incubators is mentorship. Experienced professionals and industry experts offer guidance and advice to start-up founders. Starting a business is full of pitfalls, and a good mentor can help you avoid some of the more common ones, not to mention refine your business strategies. Networking opportunities are another significant benefit of incubators. What does a new enterprise need more than anything else? Investors. Being part of an incubator program allows you to connect with potential investors, other entrepreneurs, and future business partners. Now, participating in an incubator is not without its challenges. There's a lot of competition to get into some of these programs, so not all startups are accepted. Once you've been accepted, the pressure to perform and meet milestones can be intense, and failure to do so can lose you the support of the incubator. That said, the benefits can be substantial. Incubators provide a supportive environment that fosters innovation and helps startups overcome the hurdles of early-stage development.

sections.title: 讲座 1
sections.transcript: 讲座原文： Imagine that you have a full time job, but you want to take a year off to go back to school. What is it going to cost you? Of course there's the cost of tuition for your classes, plus living expenses. But what about the money you're no longer earning at your job because you're now a student? We call that the opportunity cost. Opportunity cost refers to the value of the next best alternative that must be given up when making a choice. It's a fundamental principle in economics that helps individuals and businesses understand the true cost of their decisions. My exercise in imagination illustrates a personal decision, but businesses also face opportunity costs in their operations. For instance, a company may choose to invest in new equipment rather than spend money to expand its product line. The opportunity cost of this decision is the potential revenue that could have been generated from the new products. Understanding opportunity cost helps individuals as well as businesses make informed decisions that maximize their benefits and minimize their losses. It's important to note that opportunity cost is not always measured in financial terms. It can also be related to factors like time, convenience or personal satisfaction. For that reason, opportunity cost can be difficult to quantify, especially when dealing with non-monetary factors. Have you ever had to make a decision that included an opportunity cost? Take a few minutes now to think and then I'll ask for volunteers to share.

sections.title: 讲座 2
sections.transcript: 讲座原文： I want to tell you about an unusual phenomenon that scientists noticed in the Pacific Ocean in the early 1990's. The scientists were recording sounds using hydrophones positioned on the ocean floor in the North Pacific. Hydrophones are specially designed microphones that allow scientists to collect acoustic data underwater. While most of the undersea noises picked up by the hydrophones emanated from whales, ships engines, or earthquakes, the scientists monitoring the hydrophones detected a number of sounds that they could not identify. One was a regular series of rising infrasonic tones that is a very short wavelengths below those humans can hear. The scientists labeled these very low frequency noises up sweep. At first, these sounds were thought to be the songs of whales migrating in the Pacific. However, scientists who study whale acoustics eventually ruled out this possibility and the origin of the up sweep sounds remained unknown. So what is the source of the rising tones detected by the hydrophones? The sounds were ultimately tracked to an area of inferred volcanic seismic activity, a chain of undersea mountains in the South Pacific. Some scientists believe that if these mountains contain an active volcano, the source for the mysterious up sweep sounds may be hot volcanic lava coming in contact with cold sea water.

sections.title: 讲座 1
sections.transcript: 讲座原文： In the early 1900s, sea otters, marine mammals that feed on invertebrates including sea urchins, were nearly wiped out along the United States Pacific Coast by fur hunters. With otters gone, urchin numbers exploded, destroying kelp forests. That kelp is a type of seaweed and it's sea urchins favorite food. This left countless marine species without the protective habitat that kelp forest provided to them. In 1972, hunting sea otters was banned. As otters made a comeback, urchin numbers dropped, kelp forest grew back, and biodiversity flourished. Scientists realized otters were a keystone species, organisms whose impact on ecosystems is far greater than their numbers suggest. A similar case occurred in Yellowstone National Park. Wolves, the parks top predator, had been eradicated. Populations of elk, a deer like animal and a favorite prey for wolves, soared and their huge populations damaged local vegetation, including the Willow and Aspen trees for which the park had been famous. In the 1990s, wolves were reintroduced to the park to get the elk population under control. But the wolves didn't just cut elk numbers, they changed elk behavior. Afraid of being eaten by wolves, the elk avoided stream side areas where they're especially vulnerable. This helped Willow and Aspen trees re establish themselves there, and the trees brought back Beavers, animals that live in streams and build dams to create ponds for themselves. The Beaver dams created habitats for fish, birds and amphibians, a huge cascading effect because of this other keystone species.

sections.title: 讲座 2
sections.transcript: 讲座原文： When we think about paintings, we often focus on their subject, their style, or even the type of paint used. What we often overlook is the material underneath the paint, what we call its support or sometimes the substrate. This is the surface on which the paint is applied. The support is more important than you might think. Before the 14th century, most paintings were created on wooden panels. Wood was strong and durable, but it posed serious challenges. Large panels were extremely heavy, making transport difficult. Because of this, artists were limited in how big their works could be. Typical subjects for panel paintings were small devotional images, altar pieces, and portraits, works intended for private chapels or fixed locations rather than large public spaces. In the early 14th century, artists in Italy, especially in Venice, began turning to canvas as a support for their paintings, and by the late 15th century its use had spread widely. Canvas was light and flexible, so paintings could be moved easily and made much larger. This portability meant that monumental works could be displayed in civic buildings, palaces, and even transported for festivals. This brought art beyond the confines of churches and into broader public life. This new use of canvas wasn't just a technical change. It transformed art because it enabled ambitious subjects like vast historical scenes and mythological narratives. For example, Paulo Varanes's The Wedding at Cana, which is a massive banquet scene filled with dozens of figures and rich architectural detail.

sections.title: 讲座 1
sections.transcript: Picture a bustling town square. What makes it lively? Is it the buildings? The people? The signage? Sociologists argue that public spaces hold a mirror to a society's values. This concept, known as public sphere theory, suggests that the way we design and use our public spaces reveals much about our cultural identity. According to this theory, a city's parks, plazas, and streetscapes serve not just as physical locations, but also as stages for social interaction and cultural exchange. The theory also examines how accessible these spaces are to the people who live near them. A public space that is inclusive, one that welcomes people from all walks of life, is reflective of a progressive society. On the flip side, spaces that are restrictive or that exclude certain people are often indicative of societal divisions and inequalities. Another aspect of public sphere theory is the struggle faced by cities to balance the need for open, accessible areas with issues like overcrowding and other safety concerns. In addition, city planners often face the dilemma of preserving cultural heritage while adapting to modern needs of a community. I should note that technology is also reshaping public spaces. Social media platforms offer new arenas for interaction, and these virtual public spaces are fundamentally altering the traditional public sphere. However, just as traditional public spaces face challenges, so too do these digital spaces. Most prominent are privacy concerns and the digital divide between those who have computer access and those who do not.

sections.title: 讲座 1
sections.transcript: 1991 US District Court case Grand Upright Music Limited versus Warner Brothers Records Inc. The ruling in that case required artists to obtain permission to use samples in their recordings. Before that legal decision, sampling had been a relatively cheap and easy practice. It continued afterward, down to today, but in a more limited way. Critics often argue that sampling is a less creative approach than traditional music making, but I'd respond that all art, especially music, is referential. In creating a new work, all artists borrow in one manner or another from existing works of art. Hip hop creativity comes in finding unusual sources or putting recognizable material into new contexts. But now I'd like to know what you think. Let's examine the Sonic collage that is Paul's Boutique, the 1989 album from the Beastie Boys, which utilizes A remarkable number of samples.

sections.transcript: The main appeal of dark stores lies in their efficiency. By eliminating the traditional storefront, businesses can reduce overhead costs and pass savings on to consumers through lower prices. Their proximity to dense urban areas also allows for faster delivery times, meeting the expectations of customers who value speed and convenience. For instance, a company might delivery groceries in under an hour, giving it a major competitive advantage over traditional supermarkets. However, dark stores are not without drawbacks. Their expansion can contribute to the decline of traditional retail spaces, creating economic challenges for local businesses. Employment is another concern. While these centers generate jobs in logistics and delivery, they may reduce the number of customer-facing roles available in physical stores. Looking ahead, many experts predict that dark stores will continue to reshape the retail landscape. Some may adopt advanced automation, further reducing the need for human labor and potentially redefining the shopping experience itself. As with other technological shifts, the key challenge will be balancing efficiency with the boarder social and economic implications of these changes.

sections.transcript: Have you ever started at a blank page trying to come up with an idea of what to write about? Waiting for inspiration? Storytelling dice are a simple way to breakthrough that creative block. Yes, I'm talking about dice similar to ones you roll in some common board games to generate random numbers. But instead of numbers, each die is covered with pictorial symbols like a tree, a key, or a lightning bolt. A typical set could have nine six-sided dice. The magic lies in their unpredictability. You might roll a dragon, a locked door, and a storm. Suddenly you're weaving a tale of, say, hidden rooms and daring escapes. Storytelling dice are not just for writers. They can also serve as ice breakers at social gatherings. Imagine this. The party feels a little stiff, so you pull out the dice and say, "everyone roll three." Someone gets a dragon, a ladder, and a smiley face. Another rolls a spaceship, shoes, and a storm cloud. Soon people are laughing as they connect these random images into a wild story. The dragon was stuck on a ladder during a thunderstorm and then a spaceship landed to rescue it. It's silly, spontaneous, and gets everyone talking. But now let's get back to creative writing and talk about a short story that a previous student of mine wrote last semester. While reading the story, try to guess what three images she rolled on her dice that inspired her to write it.

sections.title: 讲座 2
sections.transcript: The age of exploration extended from the fifteenth century to the seventeenth century. But long before this, seafarers were venturing into unfamiliar waters using remarkably sophisticated technologies. One notable example is Pytheas of Massalia, a Greek explorer from the fourth century BCE. He sailed from the Mediterranean to the northern reaches of Europe, possibly reaching Britain and even Iceland. Without modern instruments, Pytheas relied on coastal landmarks, the position of the sun and stars, and careful observation of ocean tides and daylight patterns. His journey demonstrated that long-distance navigation was possible through keen environmental awareness and methodical planning. Centuries later, European explorers expanded on these early achievements with the help of new technologies. Among the most transformative was the magnetic compass, which used a magnetized needle to indicate direction. Originally developed in China and later adopted in Europe, the compass allowed sailors to maintain a heading even when celestial bodies were obscured by clouds or fog. This innovation enable mariners to venture into open seas with greater confidence and precision. Historians note that the compass didn't just improve navigation, it transformed it. It allowed explorers like Vasco da Gama and Ferdinand Magellan to chart new maritime routes across vast oceans, connecting continents and reshaping global trade. Combined with other tools like the astrolabe and improved ship designs, the compass helped usher in the age of exploration.

sections.title: 讲座 1
sections.transcript: One of the most effective strategies in modern marketing is the use of storytelling. Storytelling involves crafting a narrative around a brand or product that engages consumers on an emotional level. Instead of simply listing features and benefits, marketers use stories to create a connection with their audience, making the brand memorable and relatable. This method has been especially powerful in the age of social media, where personal stories and viral content can significantly boost brand awareness and loyalty. Successful storytelling and marketing often includes elements like a compelling character, a relatable conflict, and a satisfying resolution. For example, a company selling eco-friendly products might tell the story of a family striving to reduce their environmental footprint. This narrative not only highlights the product's benefits but also resonates with consumers who share similar values. Another aspect of storytelling and marketing is authenticity. Consumers are more likely to trust and engage with brands that appear genuine and transparent. This means that the story should reflect the brand's real values and mission, avoiding exaggeration or false claims. Visuals also play a crucial role in storytelling. High quality images and videos can bring the narrative to life, making it more impactful and easier to share. Of course, measuring the success of storytelling campaigns can be difficult, as traditional metrics like sales figures don't always capture the full impact of a well-told story.

sections.title: 讲座 2
sections.transcript: In the first half of the twentieth century, an anthropological movement emerged called the Culture and Personality school. According to the Culture and Personality school, people's personalities are a result of the culture they live in, and not just based on biology, like not just inherited from their biological parents. For example, how children in a culture experience food, the foods they eat, how it's prepared. This shapes their individual tastes and preferences. One of the anthropologists most associated with this movement was Ruth Benedict. Benedict studied and embraced the principle of cultural relativism. So according to cultural relativism, all cultures should be studied on their own terms and not judged against some external measure. So cultures in, say, Egypt belong to Egypt and shouldn't be the standard of what all cultures should try to be. Ruth Benedict refuted the dominant anthropology theory at the time, which stated that there was a hierarchy of cultures, some advanced, others not. Rejecting that took courage, and I think the field is better for it. Benedict was also influenced by psychology, especially Gestalt ideas. According to Gestalt's psychology, a personality is an integrated whole, not just a list of traits. Like if you see a painting of a landscape, you're looking at a whole landscape and not just, say, a hill, trees, and a farmhouse. Benedict said that cultures were the same way, a whole coherent system with patterns of values and behaviors and more than just a set of characteristics.

sections.title: 讲座 1
sections.transcript: Let's talk a little about sea otters and their importance to their own and indeed other ecosystems. We'll start with a few basic facts. The sea otter is a marine mammal often found along the coastal waters of the northern Pacific. It lacks the blubber of other marine mammals like whales, say, or seals, but it stays warm in icy waters thanks to its fur, which is the densest of any animals. It also has unusually large lungs, two-and-a-half times larger than those of similarly sized land mammals, and this helps it stay buoyant and dive efficiently. Sea otters have a loose flap of skin under each forearm that functions like a pocket, which they use for storing food and tools. That's right, tools. Sea otters are one of the few animals that use tools, using clam shells for digging and rocks to open clam shells. Now, wonderful as they maybe, why care about sea otters? Because sea otters eat sea urchins, and sea urchins eat kelp. Kelp is a large seaweed that can grow up to thirty meters tall, providing food and shelter for a range of marine life. Kelp forests support a greater variety of marine life than almost any other ocean habitats. Kelp also grows very densely and acts as a natural buffer, protecting shorelines from storm damage. Finally, kelp forests are like rainforests in that they absorb and store carbon dioxide through photosynthesis, mitigating climate change and reducing ocean acidification.

sections.title: 讲座 2
sections.transcript: Have you ever listened to a piece of music and felt like you were suddenly somewhere else? Maybe walking through a Brazilian street market or climbing a misty mountain trail in China? That's the magic of musical borrowing, a practice where artists blend elements from different global traditions to create something fresh and emotionally resonant. Take bossa Nova, for example. It's a genre that merges the laid back swing of United States jazz music with the rhythmic pulse of Brazilian samba. When you listen to bossa Nova, it feels both familiar and new at the same time. But successful musical borrowing isn't just about mixing sounds. It's about respect. When artists draw from other cultures, they need to understand the traditions behind the music. Composer Tan Dun nails this in his score for the film Crouching Tiger, Hidden Dragon. He blends Chinese instruments like the Erhu and PIPA with Western orchestration, but not just for effect. The Erhu's haunting tones and the Pipa's intricate rhythms reflect centuries of Chinese musical storytelling. Tan Dun doesn't just borrow, he honors the culture, letting its emotional depth shine through. Of course, fusion isn't always seamless. Sometimes the mix feels forced, or the original meaning gets lost. But when it works, when the traditions truly speak to each other, it's proof that music can be a universal language, capable of bridging worlds and telling stories that transcend borders.

sections.title: 讲座 2
sections.transcript: Nanoparticles are particles, whose size is less than one ten-thousandth of a millimeter, super tiny. Nanoparticles have numerous applications. My family had a picnic last Saturday, we used sunscreen to avoid sunburn. Our sunscreen contains titanium dioxide which has been used in sunscreen for decades. You used to end up with these horrible-looking white smears all over your skin while wearing it. But our new sunscreen's titanium dioxide comes in nanoparticles. They block ultraviolet sunlight but are transparent. The sun block's completely invisible on your skin, not smeary white. Another example, the metal silver has antimicrobial properties. The problem is, you can't put regular metal on a wound. But an ointment with silver nanoparticles, we can actually apply that to stop bacterial growth. We did it when my son scraped his knee at the picnic. Humans have actually used nanoparticles for millennia. Take ancient Rome's tesserae. Tesserae are tiny bits of highly colorful glass that the Romans arranged to create various images. Many Roman tesserae, especially pink ones, contain gold nanoparticles. The particles affect how light interacts with the glass and create the color. Did the Romans know what they were doing? Well, they probably didn't understand the physics of it. But some glass workshop could have realized that gold foil, beaten to an extremely thin layer, produces bright colors when heated between glass layers, and the technique was perfected and spread. All pink tesserae contain gold nanoparticles at between ten and thirty parts per million. That's so consistent. So it's definitely not an accident. The Romans knew exactly what they were doing to produce that color.

sections.transcript: Welcome to the world of kinetic art, a mesmerizing fusion of motion and visual storytelling. Born in the early twentieth century, kinetic art is still pushing boundaries, constantly redefining what art can be. Unlike static paintings or marble sculptures, kinetic pieces come alive. Think of Alexander Calder's Mobiles delicately balanced to sway with the air. Or Theo Jansen's strand beest, giant wind-powered creatures that walk across beaches like living machines. These works don't just sit there. They respond. They evolve. Hungarian artist Laszlo Moholy-Nagy, one of the movement's pioneers, believed light and motion could transform how we experience art. Moholy-Nagy created a ground-breaking piece called Light Space Modulator, a motorized sculpture of spinning metal and glass, more of a performance than an object. But kinetic art isn't all smooth sailing. Incorporating motors and sensors means dealing with breakdowns, software glitches and constant upkeep. Some critics argue that the tech can overshadow the artistry, turning installations into flashy gimmicks. Still, the genre thrives. From interactive digital landscapes to whimsical mechanical sculptures, kinetic art invites us into a multisensory experience, one that's immersive, unpredictable and unforgettable.

sections.transcript: These organisms break down organic material into a dark, crumbly, earthy smelling substance called humus. Unlike decomposition in landfills, composting occurs aerobically, or with oxygen, and therefore it doesn't produce methane gas. To compost effectively, you need the right balance of four things. One is nitrogen-rich materials, also known as greens, things like fruit and vegetable scraps. The second one is carbon-rich materials, or browns, like dry leaves, wood chips and paper waste, and you also need water and air. So, the process does require proper management. Human, the primary product of composting, is full of essential nutrients. Adding it to soil enhances plant growth and increases agricultural yields. This reduces the need for chemical fertilizers. Human enriches soil also provides a habitat for microorganisms, insects, and worms that, in turn, help decompose organic material and maintain soil health. This creates a virtuous circle of soil. In contrast, while chemical fertilizers can boost agricultural productivity in the short term, they are harmful to these beneficial organisms. They can actually damage the soil in the long run by killing the helpful organisms living in it.

sections.transcript: Maybe, like most people, you think of an inventor alone in his laboratory, tinkering with devices that no one else had ever dreamed of. Well, actually, there were often multiple people working on similar inventions at once. They'd improve on each other's work, compete or collaborate. Have you heard of Lewis Latimer, who invented one kind of early air-conditioner and improved the toilet systems in trains? Probably not. Latimer, as a black man, was excluded from many opportunities that his white peers enjoyed in the United States. He never even got to attend high school, but he taught himself, uh, practiced on his own, to be a drafter, someone who makes technical drawings. Latimer's drawings were so skillful they were practically works of art. He wrote poetry, and you can see his poetic sensitivity even in his drafting work. Anyway, after practicing to learn drafting. Latimer worked with several famous inventors over the span of his career. One was Hiram Maxim. Working with Hiram Maxim, Latimer developed and patented a major innovation in carbon filaments. Um, a carbon filament is a thin wire inside a light bulb that glows with electricity to produce light. Latimer made these filaments stronger and longer-lasting and easier to make. This was a major step in making lighting feasible and affordable for the general public.

sections.transcript: Ephesus includes massive remains from different time periods, including Roman, Greek, and Byzantine periods, which are different civilizations spanning millennia. For example, at Ephesus there are ruins of ancient Greek temples and Roman theaters. Other archaeological sites, though, are more difficult to reach. There's an entire subfield of archaeology that focuses on these sites. It's called underwater archaeology. Underwater archaeology is the study of human history through sites and artifacts found beneath the water's surface. This includes shipwrecks, submerged settlements, harbors, and ports. Researchers have found all kinds of artifacts at underwater sites, including tools, pottery, coins, and other objects. Because water can slow decay, especially of organic materials like wood or textiles, underwater sties often provide exceptionally well-preserved evidence of past human activity. One notable underwater site the Uluburun shipwreck off the coast of Turkey, dating to about three-thousand years ago. Uluburun was discovered in 1982. Specialized diving and excavation techniques were used at this site and archaeologists recovered cargo including copper ingot and luxury goods. These artifacts shed light on ancient trade networks. They suggest that highly complex multi-regional trade routes connecting Central Asia to Europe and Africa existed far earlier than we expected.

sections.title: 讲座 1
sections.transcript: (man) Frogs aren’t just known for their croaks and leaps. They’re key players in ecosystems, acting as both predators and prey, but scientists have been sounding the alarm. Frog population are shrinking fast across the globe. One major reason is chemical pollution. Pesticides and other pollutants often end up in the water where frogs live and breed. These chemicals interfere with their reproductive systems, leading to fewer eggs and developmental issues in tadpoles. Over time, this can cause entire population to collapse. Another serious threat is disease, especially a fungus called Chytrid. This fungus attacks the skin of frogs, which is vital for absorbing water and regulating electrolytes. Infected frogs often become lethargic, lose coordination, and eventually die. Chytrid has spread rapidly and is responsible for declines and extinctions in hundreds of frog species worldwide. It’s one of the most devastating wildlife diseases ever recorded. Why is this problematic? Frogs also serve as indicators of environmental health. Because they’re so sensitive to changes in water quality and temperature, their decline often signals deeper ecological problems. Bees play a similar role. When bee populations drop, it can point to issues like pesticide overuse or habitat stress. So when frogs and bees are struggling, it’s a warning sign that the environment needs attention.

sections.title: 讲座 2
sections.transcript: (woman) Last week, we talked about realism, in which artists aimed to depict the world as it really exists. Today, we’ll explore surrealism. Starting in France in the 1920s, surrealist artists focused on inner realities, concepts such as fantasy and the nature of dreams. Their works reflected a combination of these inner realities as well as outer realities, that is, things we physically experience. Their paintings often depicted a familiar scene, but in a dreamlike manner. Spaniard Joan Miro was especially adept at surrealism. Interestingly, though, Miro never wanted to be associated with any artistic movement, and he never called himself a surrealist, but his contemporaries did, and we can see why they did when we look at Miro’s work. Miro typically painted in two stages. The latter stage was carefully calculated. It was meticulous and precise. Miro knew exactly what he was doing in this stage. But in the initial stage, Miro didn’t plan what he was going to paint. He just started painting. The form, whatever it was, a bird, a building, whatever appeared on the canvas, the form suggested itself under his brush. That’s how Miro described it. This method of creating art without conscious control is called automatism. Automatism is quite noticeable in a work of Miro’s that is titled, simply, Painting. Even Miro couldn’t fully explain the meaning of this work. Presumably the images that appeared came from things deep inside him, things he may not have even known were there.

sections.title: 讲座 1
sections.transcript: (woman) Today, we’re exploring a fascinating concept in social science known as pluralistic ignorance. Pluralistic ignorance describes a situation where the majority of members in a group privately reject a norm or standard, but assume incorrectly that most others accept it. This often results in everyone conforming to a norm they don’t truly agree with. A classic example occurs in workplace overtime culture. Many employees might prefer to leave work on time, but they stay late because they believe everyone else is committed to working extra hours. In reality, most colleagues also wish to leave on time but fear appearing less dedicated. Research highlights this dynamic. When employees are asked privately about their preferences, many express a desire for better work-life balance despite their public behavior suggesting enthusiasm for long hours. Pluralistic ignorance has broad implications well beyond the workplace. Notably, it can perpetuate social stereotypes and hinder societal change, as individuals might hesitate to voice dissenting opinions, thinking they’re in the minority. However, overcoming pluralistic ignorance has powerful benefits. When even one person speaks up, it can embolden others to express their true beliefs, potentially leading to a shift in group norms and to more honest, authentic communities. But there’s a challenge and it’s a big one. Being the first to speak out often requires courage, as it can risk one’s social standing among one’s peers.

sections.title: 讲座 2
sections.transcript: (man) Today, we’re going to explore a phenomenon called thin film interference. This is an optical effect that occurs when light interacts with very thin surfaces. Imagine a soap bubble floating in the air. Although it’s made of clear liquid, it shines with shifting rainbow colors. Thin film interference explains how this shimmering display occurs. When light strikes a bubble, some reflects off the outer surface and some reflects off the inner surface. As these waves meet, they can either work together or work against each other. If they reinforce one another, the color looks brighter. This is called constructive interference because the waves are constructing, or building, the light. If the waves hit each other and cancel each other out, the color fades. This is destructive interference because the waves are destroying each other’s effect. Which color appears depends on factors that keep changing, factors like the thickness of the film and the angle of the light. As these factors shift, some wavelengths are reinforced while others are cancelled and that constant change is what produces the bubble’s rainbow shimmer. The thin film that creates these dazzling colors also makes the bubble fragile. Because the layer is so delicate, the bubble can burst with the slightest touch or breeze. Scientists are interested in applying thin film interference to technology. Possible uses include paints that shine with bright colors without pigments and anti-reflective coatings for lenses. Yet reproducing the bubble's natural balance of simplicity and efficieny remains a significant challenge.

sections.transcript: When you think of Siberia, you picture a cold place. But in 2014, Siberia had an unusually warm summer. Attempts exceeded 30°C a couple times. And also in 2014, a helicopter pilot flying over a particular area of Siberia spotted a strange crater, a cylindrical hole in the ground that was massive, 20 meters wide and 50 meters deep. Really huge. Following the report, scientists investigated and found more such craters in the same area. It looked like stuff had just exploded from the ground, with material flying out and landing hundreds of meters away. These explosions occurred in an area where oil and gas extraction take place, so they're a real concern. What if an explosion happens near an oil or gas pipeline? What's happening is connected to the warmer temperatures. Let's back up. The region's soil is permanently frozen. It's called permafrost with pockets of ice in it. This permafrost is on top of an extensive field of underground natural gas. The ice and permafrost help hold the gas under the surface, but warming temperatures 'cause melting at the surface, so it can't seal the gas underground as effectively. Also, when the ice in the permafrost melts, it leaves behind empty cavities where the ice used to be. What's probably happening is the gas from below rises up and fills these cavities, building up the pressure. Eventually the gas bursts through and boom a crater, causing explosion.These craters are called gas emission craters.

sections.title: 讲座 1
sections.transcript: Welcome to Echoes of Culture, where we explore how music tells the story of who we are, where we've been, and where we're going. Today, we're diving into a fascinating idea how musical composition mirrors the societies from which it emerges. Music is more than just sounds. It is a reflection of cultural values, technological progress, and social change. Let's rewind to the Baroque. Picture the grandeur of European courts, ornate architecture, lavish clothing, and a love for complexity. Composers weren't just writing music, they were crafting sonic tapestries that mirrored the opulence of their time. Elaborate counterpoint, intricate ornamentation. These weren't just stylistic choices. They were reflections of a society that valued structure, hierarchy and beauty and excess. Fast forward to the 20th century and the musical landscape shifts dramatically. Jazz bursts onto the scene in the United States, and it's not just a new genre, it's a movement. Born in African American communities, jazz carried the pulse of a society in flux. It's improvisational nature and blending of traditions spoke to a yearning for freedom, innovation and equality. Jazz became the soundtrack of the Civil Rights movement, echoing the struggles and triumphs of a people demanding to be heard. And it's not just Western music that tells these stories. In sub-Saharan Africa, traditional music is deeply communal, less about individual display and more about shared experience. The emphasis on group expression is woven into the rhythms, the call and response, interaction between performers and audiences, and communal participation.

sections.title: 讲座 2
sections.transcript: Have you ever wondered why certain urban neighborhoods flourish while others stagnate? A fascinating theory known as the creative class offers one explanation. Coined by sociologist Richard Florida, this concept suggests that cities with a high concentration of creative professionals, including artists, scientists, and entrepreneurs, tend to experience more significant economic growth and revitalization. The idea is that these individuals Dr. innovation and attract others like them, creating a vibrant, dynamic atmosphere. However, it's important to note that such a transformation isn't without its drawbacks. When these creative hubs thrive economically, it can inadvertently lead to gentrification. That is, it can cause rising property values and living costs. This often displaces long standing residents who can no longer afford to live in their own neighborhoods. This process can erode the unique cultural fabric that made the area attractive in the 1st place. Despite this, cities continue to pursue the creative class strategy. They invest in cultural infrastructure like galleries and performance spaces. The lure creative professionals. Yet critics argue that this focus on attracting the creative class might over shadow the needs of other community members, particularly those in lower income brackets. It's a delicate balancing act that cities must navigate carefully, fostering economic vitality while ensuring inclusivity and equity. So next time you stroll through a bustling urban district filled with lively cafes and art installations, consider the multifaceted dynamics at play that underpin its success.

sections.title: 讲座 1
sections.transcript: (man) When we think of the Renaissance, we often picture grand paintings and sculptures, but a lesserknown art form also flourished during this period, tapestry weaving. Tapestries were not only decorative pieces, but also served practical purposes such as insulating the cold stone walls of castles. Artists of the era used tapestries to depict intricate scenes from mythology, religion, and daily life, often incorporating vibrant colors and rich textures. An advantage of tapestries was their portability. Unlike frescos, which were fixed to walls, tapestries could be rolled up and transported from one location to another, allowing their owners to display their wealth wherever they went. This portability also had a downside, however. Tapestries were susceptible to damage during transit. Even today, museums face challenges preserving these unique artworks due to their fragile nature. The creation of a tapestry was a laborintensive process requiring collaboration between designers, weavers and dyers. Unlike paintings, which could be completed by a single artist, tapestries were team efforts and it was common for a designer’s sketches to be translated by skilled weavers into woven masterpieces. The intricate craftsmanship required to produce these artworks offers a glimpse into the collaborative spirit of the Renaissance era.

sections.title: 讲座 2
sections.transcript: (man) I once saw a video of a lionfish with its intimidating long spikes. Then it suddenly turned into a snake. Well, it turned out I was actually watching a mimic octopus. The mimic octopus lives in relatively shallow ocean water, and it’s the first animal known to show dynamic mimicry, which means it can shift quickly between multiple imitations. Now, other creatures use mimicry. The owl butterfly’s wings have markings resembling an owl’s eye, which may keep the butterfly’s predators away. But that’s how the owl butterfly always looks. With dynamic mimicry, by contrast, an animal can shift its shape in real time. It concocts its body into different formations, often to confuse predators. A mimic octopus can imitate a lionfish or a snake, and it can quickly extend its arms and glide across the sea floor like a flatfish. But what use is changing shape if you can’t also change color to look like a flatfish? Well, this octopus has cells called chromatophores just under its skin. Each chromatophore has a pigment inside it that could be red, yellow, et cetera. Uh, picture thousands of tiny balloons of different colors. If you stretch a balloon, it gets bigger, right? Well, the mimic octopus has muscles surrounding these chromatophores. They tighten to pull the necessary colors bigger and relax to make other colors smaller, making each color more or less visible. While this helps it hide from predators, it also aids in hunting as unsuspecting prey often perceives the octopus as a nonthreatening species.

sections.title: 讲座 1
sections.transcript: (woman) Today, we're going to talk about the importance of wetlands and their role in ecosystems. Wetlands are areas where water covers the soil, either permanently or seasonally, and include marshes, swamps, and bogs. These are incredibly productive ecosystems that provide numerous benefits to the environment and human society. They serve as critical habitats for a wide variety of wildlife, including birds, fish, and amphibians. And they provide breeding grounds and food sources that are essential for the survival of many species. But wetlands aren't just waterlogged habitat, they're biochemical powerhouses. One of their primary functions is to act as natural water filters, breaking down or neutralizing toxic substances like heavy metals and pesticides through the action of specialized microbes. These microbial communities form complex relationships with plants and sediments, creating a natural filtration system that can detoxify pollutants before they reach rivers, lakes, or groundwater. Another significant role of wetlands is their ability to manage floodwaters. During periods of heavy rain, wetlands can absorb and store excess water, reducing the risk of floods in surrounding areas. Furthermore, wetlands are important for carbon sequestration, capturing and storing large amounts of carbon dioxide, which helps mitigate climate change. However, wetlands face numerous threats, including drainage from agriculture, urban development, and pollution. Protecting and restoring wetlands is crucial for maintaining their ecological functions and the benefits they provide. In the next part of our class, we will examine specific efforts to conserve and restore wetlands around the world.

sections.title: 讲座 2
sections.transcript: (man) Construction materials have changed significantly over the centuries. The desire to employ more sustainable, more environmentallyfriendly building methods in recent years has led to advances in what we use for construction. For example, there's actually a new building in Amsterdam in the Netherlands whose structure is made with concrete that captures carbon from the atmosphere. And as you know, capturing atmospheric carbon helps mitigate global warming. However, a building technique doesn't need to be newly invented to be environmentally friendly. In fact, an ancient building technique involving the use of adobe bricks is making a comeback. So, what's good about it? Well, for starters, adobe bricks are made from simple natural materials, clay, sand, water, and sometimes organic fibers. They're shaped and left to dry in the sun, which means we skip the energyheavy manufacturing process. Pretty efficient, right? Adobe also has an amazing ability to regulate temperature. Its thermal mass absorbs heat during the day and slowly releases it at night. That means less need for air conditioning and more natural comfort. Adobe's insulation really shines in some places in the southwestern United States, which experience huge temperature fluctuations and where native populations made adobe from local materials and used it thousands of years ago. Today's builders are rediscovering adobe as it blends tradition with sustainability. Using local materials cuts down on transportation costs and emissions, so less need for transportation is another thing that makes adobe ecofriendly.

sections.transcript: (man) Today, we're exploring the luminous world of stained glass. When you think of stained glass, you probably think of windows in churches, but it is found outside of churches as well. If fact, it used to brighten many homes across the United States. In the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries, stained glass windows became a beloved feature in domestic architecture thanks to the Arts and Crafts movement. The Arts and Crafts movement celebrated craftsmanship and natural beauty, and stained glass fit the bill perfectly. Artists used several techniques to bring their visions to life. The lead method, a traditional approach, involved joining pieces of glass with strips of lead, ideal for bold geometric designs. Then came the copper foil technique, popularized by the American artist and designer Louis Comfort Tiffany. This method wrapped each glass piece in thin copper foil, which allowed for more intricate designs like floras and landscapes. But these beautiful windows weren't without drawbacks. They often lack proper insulation, leading to heat loss in colder climates. Home owners had to weigh aesthetics against practicality, sometimes adding storm windows or heavy drapes to compensate. Stained glass windows eventually faded from popularity in domestic architecture, but they're enjoying a quiet renaissance in contemporary art. Modern artists blend old techniques with new technologies like laser cutting, digital design and fused-glass methods to create contemporary pieces for homes, galleries and the public spaces.

sections.title: 讲座 2
sections.transcript: (man) Imagine an ancient garden or field and imagine organic material in its soil, things like plant roots or wooden irrigation pipes. When this organic material decays over the centuries, it often leaves behind voids in the soil. Researchers can fill these voids by injecting plaster into the empty spaces. When the plaster hardens, it creates casts, essentially three-dimensional negatives that replicate what existed centuries ago. For example, at the ancient Maya village of Hoya de Siren in El Salvador, Central America, casts taken from root cavities have revealed a diverse mix of crops, including manioc, maize and beans. These species were identified in part by the shape and size of the root voids, by comparing them with modern plant root systems. This layout of plants in the garden wasn't random at all. It showed the garden to be an early example of the Milpa system, a traditional intercropping method still practiced in Central America and Mexico today, with a tall maize plants provides stalks for bean plants to climb. The beans enrich the soil with nitrogen and squash plants growing along the ground provide shade that suppresses weeds and retains moisture. Soil casts have also been used at the sites of ancient Roman villa gardens, revealing irrigation channels and beds planted with species such as grape vines and roses. The findings show a deliberate integration of ornamental plants with edible plants, suggesting a Roman design ethos that sought to balance aesthetics with utility.

sections.transcript: (woman) Let's move on in our renewable energy series to discuss solar power, which is arguably the most abundant resource available. Solar power takes energy from the sun's rays and coverts it to electricity or heat. The primary technology for this is solar panels made up of photovoltaic cells, which generate an electric current when sunlight hits them. The advantages of solar power are well known, and the most important may be the fact that it produces zero pollutants. Any industrial endeavor will produce carbon dioxide in one way or another, and manufacturing solar panels itself requires energy sourced from fossil fuels. But on the whole, the industry has a much lower carbon footprint than coal or natural gas, and this makes it key to reducing greenhouse gas emissions. Another advantage, and we don't talk about enough, is that solar power can provide energy access in remote and underserved areas far from the grid. So what are the disadvantages? Solar panel efficiency is affected by cloud cover and other weather, which, of course, reduces the amount of sunlight reaching the panels. That said, innovations in battery storage systems do allow for the storage of solar energy for use during non-sunny periods. Panel lifespan is quite good at twenty-five to thirty years, but improvements in efficiency are paradoxically driving panels to be replaced much earlier than that, so waste is increasing faster than expected. This is a problem because recycling them is expensive and most panels end up in landfills.

sections.transcript: (man) The Galapagos Islands, a popular tourist attraction located approximate one-thousand kilometers off mainland Ecuador, have long been home to many interesting species of animals, including giant tortoises. Historically, these reptiles could be found on many different Galapagos Islands, but in some of these locations they've gone extinct due in part to human activities. To deal with this situation, conservationists employed a strategy called animal translocation, to move tortoises from one island to another. So, why did conservationists do this? The main reason was to promote ecosystem recovery on affected islands. One place tortoises went extinct was on Santa Fe Island. When these reptiles died out, the island was without its main ecosystem engineer. This affected the island in many ways, including causing plant diversity to decline. To help the ecosystem recover, conservationists have released more than four-hundred tortoises from Espanola Island to Fanta Fe Island. This was done to help restore natural processes like seed dispersal and vegetation control. The goal is to reach about four-thousand individuals to match historical densities. And there are signs that this project is having success. For example, a type of cactus that many animals on the island rely on for food has shown improved reproduction and growth since the tortoises returned. This is not doubt because tortoises eat this cactus's fruit and spread seeds in their nutrient-rich droppings. This finding is encouraging, but we can't declare the project of victory yet. More time needs to pass before conservationists can deem it a success.

sections.transcript: (man) There are many species out there that we wouldn't expect to see flying, mammals, reptiles. One fascinating creature is the flying squid. Now, squid have fins, arms, tentacles, and gills for breathing. Their main body, the mantle, is basically a tube of muscle that water goes inside of while they swim. When this mantle shuts it, it pumps the water out, which propels the squid through water quite quickly. It's like a little jet pack, and, uh, flying squid are able to propel themselves right up through the ocean surface and into the air above. Another unexpected flying creature is the flying squirrel, which can simply glide, sometimes quickly and for long distances between tree branches. However, unlike the flying squirrel, flying squid not only glides but can actually propel themselves upward and, well, a flying squid can accelerate as fast as a car, getting up to one-hundred kilometers per hour in about a second. Then, the squid extends its tentacles and arms, and it has membranes between them that spread out and help the squid glide for several seconds, a bit like temporary wings. A squid in flight is likely to be fleeing from an underwater predator or a ship. There are some alternative theories, though. One is that it's a migration strategy, since moving through the air takes less energy and time than moving through water.

sections.transcript: (man) In the nineteenth century, cities in the United States became crowded. Many businesses and apartments were housed in tall buildings. Fires became a major concern. Most fire track ladders only reached the fourth floor, which wasn't high enough. Although laws were passed to require escape routes, many early ideas were impractical. Like one idea was to attach a parachute to your head. A parachute idea? Well, this wouldn't work too well, would it? Other such ideas were met with resistance, too. Enter Anna Connolly, who received patents for fire escapes in the nineteenth century. Anna Connolly's initial fire escape design was a bridge so people could safely go up to the roof or upper floors of their own building, cross to the building next door, and go down the stairs there. This made good sense since most fires started on the lower floors of buildings. After this design, Connelly created another that was a series of platforms attached to the side of a building with ladders connecting to them. She specified they'd be made of iron, since iron is fireproof and resists pressure. Well, this design worked, was practical, and was adopted across the country. Connolly's fire escapes saved lives. These days, buildings in the US are built with interior stairwells that are fireproof for escape and are not visible from the outside, but you can still see Connolly's design on older buildings in cities.
