sections.transcript: (woman) In 1967, astronomer Carl Sagan and biology Harold Morowitz published a provocative paper in the journal Nature. At the time, most scientists assumed extraterrestrial life could only exist on planets with Earth-like surfaces, moderate temperatures, liquid water and a solid ground to stand on. Sagan and Morowitz challenged that assumption. They argued that while Venus's surface is far too hot for life, hot enough to melt lead, the planet's upper cloud layers were a different story. About fifty kilometers above the surface, temperatures and pressures resemble those on Earth's surface. They speculated that microbial life could survive in those clouds, floating in droplets of sulfuric acid and water vapor, adapted to extreme acidity and using sunlight as a source of energy. To make their case, Sagan and Morowitz pointed to early analogs, microbes thriving in the acidic hot springs of Yellowstone National Park in the United States. These springs are pools heated by geothermal energy, rich in minerals and often highly acidic. Yet certain extremophiles, microbes adapted to harsh conditions, flourish there, using chemical reactions to survive. If life can adapt to boiling acidic water on Earth, they reasoned, why not to acidic clouds on Venus? Their argument was speculative, but it cracked open the idea that life is not confined to Earth-like surfaces, which is significant because a large percentage of the planets in the universe don't even have a solid surface at all.

sections.title: 讲座 2
sections.transcript: (man) If you were to take a walk in the Arctic tundra, you'd be walking over permafrost, a soil layer that has remained frozen for thousands of years. As global temperatures rise, however, the stability of this permafrost is compromised. And this brings something into play that you might not expect, microbes. Now, you might wonder, why does such tiny organisms even matter? It's because when permafrost thaws, dormant microbes activate and decompose organic material, releasing greenhouse gases like carbon dioxide and methane. OK, so this actually initiates a feedback loop. The emission of gases accelerates warming, and that warming leads to further thawing of permafrost. This kind of cycle is a relatively recent discovery, and it's more influential than previously assumed. To put it in perspective, permafrost holds about double the carbon present in the entire atmosphere. This means we have to understand microbial activities if we want to forecast future climate trends. To address this issue, researchers use sophisticated models analyzing a number of elements, including the specific microbial species in these thawing soils. But what are the implications if these feedback loops persist? Well, it could lead to a significant rise in atmospheric greenhouse gases, intensifying global warming.

sections.title: 讲座 1
sections.transcript: Listen to a lecture in an art history class. 听力原文：(woman) Let's talk about a classic example of land art, Spiral Jetty by Robert Smithson. Picture yourself at the edge of the Great Salt Lake in the state of Utah in the United States. Stretching out into the water is a massive spiral made of dark basalt rocks about one-thousand-five-hundred feet long. The title tells you a lot. A jetty is a structure that sticks out into a body of water, usually to protect a shoreline or dock. Smithson took that idea and twisted it, literally, into a spiral. Land art is an art movement that wanted to break free from museums and galleries and put art directly into nature. Smithson was fascinated by big concepts like geological time and change. He never intended Spiral Jetty to be permanent. The lake rises and falls, salt crystals form on the rocks and the spiral slowly transforms. He wanted people to experience that reality firsthand, to make the journey and see the work in its natural setting. Here's the irony, though. Relatively few people have actually seen Spiral Jetty firsthand. Most people know it only through photographs and films that have been made about it. All this undermines Smithson's idea because the work is supposedly about being there, about sensing its scale and its shifting relationship with the Great Salt Lake. When we only see pictures, it becomes a static image, raising questions about whether land art, or at least this particular example of land art, can actually ever fulfill its intent.

sections.title: 讲座 2
sections.transcript: 听力原文：(man) Linguists have designed experiments to study infant language learning. Take the now famous WUG test. In the test, a child is shown a drawing of a made-up creature called a wug. Then they're shown two of them and asked, “Now, there are two?” Most children say wugs, adding the plural s, although they're never heard the word before. This shows young kids not only memorize words, but apply grammatical rules to words they've never heard before. Another study how babies learn word boundaries. From the sound of spoken language, it isn't obvious where one word ends and another begins. You can tell that only if you already know a lot about the language. So how can children pick out words and learn them? In an experiment, eight-month-old infants listened to a stream of made-up syllables with no pauses. After two minutes, researchers tested the babies using the head-turn preference method. They played two types of audio, one with sound patterns that are like real words and that is appeared frequently in the stream, and another with random syllables. Babies tended to turn their heads and listen longer to the familiar sounds. This showed that they had picked up on statistical patterns, like which syllables tended to follow each other, and use that to segment speech. Turns out babies are highly sophisticated pattern seekers. This suggests language learning might be linked to other cognitive abilities like attention and memory. Do they correlate? Let's discuss some studies on that next.

sections.title: 讲座 1
sections.transcript: 听力原文：(man) Let's talk about how ideas and values are transmitted across national borders, leading to an interconnected and interdependent world. This process, known as cultural globalization, has been going on for millennia, but it has been accelerated by advancements in communication, technology, and transportation. Certainly one of the most visible aspects of cultural globalization is the spread of popular culture. Movies, music, fashion, and food from one part of the world often become popular in other regions. American films, for instance, are watched all over the world, and American fast food chains are found in numerous countries as well. This diffusion of culture can lead to greater cultural understanding and exchange, fostering a sense of global community. However, if also raises concerns about the erosion of local cultures and identities. The dominance of Western culture, in particular, can overshadow indigenous traditions and practices, leading to worldwide cultural homogenization. This can result in the loss of cultural diversity, as unique customs and languages may fade away. There's also the issue of cultural appropriation. Cultural appropriation occurs when elements of one culture are taken and used by another, often without understanding and respect. On the other hand, cultural globalization can empower cultures by providing platforms for them to reach a global audience.

sections.title: 讲座 2
sections.transcript: 听力原文：(woman) When we study ecosystems, we're not just looking at a collection of plants and animals scattered across the landscape, we're diving into a dynamic web of interactions, all of which shape the structure and function of the natural world. One particularly fascinating concept within this field is that of keystone species. In architecture, a keystone is a central stone that locks an arch together. Remove it and the arch collapses. Similarly, a keystone species has a disproportionately large effect on its environment. It cannot be removed without threatening the whole ecosystem. A striking example is the gray wolf in Yellowstone National Park in the US. In the early twentieth century, wolves were eradicated from the region due to widespread hunting through government predator control programs driven by concerns over livestock and human safety. Without wolves, elk populations, you probably know elk are a type of deer that wolves hunt and eat, um, the elk population surged dramatically with their main predator gone. And all these elk, which eat many kinds of vegetation, began overgrazing, which suppressed the growth of trees and other plants in the area. This destabilized the whole ecosystem. Birds had fewer places to nest, mice and rabbits couldn't use plants to hide from predators, and even bees had fewer flowers to feed from. When wolves were reintroduced in the 1990s, their presence reshaped the landscape. Elk populations decreased, which allowed plant and tree populations to recover and, in turn, all the animals who depended on them.

sections.transcript: Listen to part of a talk at an art class. 听力原文：(woman) Today, we’re going to look at an interesting intersection between art and music. Now, you might have heard of the Russian abstract painter Wassily Kandinsky. What you might not know is how the work of an avant-garde composer, Arnold Schoenberg, influenced Kandinsky’s groundbreaking approach to painting. OK, early in the twentieth century, Wassily Kandinsky was influenced by the music of Arnold Schoenberg, a pioneer in the realm of atonality, a musical approach where there is no key. Atonality is a stark divergence from the conventions of the time where traditional tonal structures were popular. Schoenberg’s rebellion against these norms sparked Kandinsky’s imagination, which prompted him to transcend the confines of realistic representation in his art. Kandinsky thought that color and form could evoke emotions as powerfully as musical notes played by an orchestra. For example, he believed that a sharp red triangle could feel as tense or exciting as a sudden blast of trumpets. It was Schoenberg’s departure from musical tradition that inspired Kandinsky to experiment with color and form, which led to his pioneering contributions to Abstract Expressionism. This interplay between music and visual art underscores the notion that creativity is not confined within strict boundaries. Creativity can be a dynamic relationship across domains. So, Kandinsky’s artworks, they were inspired by Schoenberg’s compositions, and they serve as a reminder that the essence of art can be as fluid as the melodies that inspire it.

sections.title: 讲座 2
sections.transcript: 听力原文：(man) Soil isn’t just dirt, it’s alive. In healthy soil, microorganisms like bacteria and fungi help break down organic matter and cycle nutrients like nitrogen and phosphorus, which plants need to thrive. Not only that, but microbes create sticky substances called extracellular polymeric substances that bind soil particles together. Extracellular polymeric substances are important for maintaining soil structure, which means proper water retention, aeration, and root growth. Without microbes, soil becomes compacted, dry, and less able to support life. Now, when we’re trying to reverse damage to a degraded ecosystem, say a forest that’s been logged or farmland that’s been overused, microbes can be key players. Scientists engaged in these efforts often begin by studying a reference site. A reference site is a nearby area that shows what the ecosystem should look like in its healthy state. For example, if they’re restoring a grassland, they’ll look at an untouched patch of native grassland. They’ll analyze the soil there, its nutrients, texture and microbial communities to determine what’s missing in the damaged site. After this research comes the intervention phase. Scientists might introduce microbial inoculants, custom blends of helpful microbes, to the degraded soil. These microbes rebuild structure, cycle nutrients and support plant growth. In one California vineyard, years of chemical use had depleted microbial diversity and compacted the soil, making it hard for vines to thrive. Researchers introduced various fungi and other beneficial microbes. Within a year, the soil structure improved, water retention increased, and grape yield and quality noticeably rebounded.

But before her death in 1954, she was mainly known as the wife of another famous artist, Diego Rivera, and critics and the public barely heard of her until decades later, probably not until a Hollywood movie about her life in 2002. These days, Frida Kahlo’s best known artworks are her paintings, especially her self-portraits showing her with a serious expression, thick eyebrows and traditional Mexican cloths. Kahlo’s drawings, however, are rather obscure, even now. One drawing, a self-portrait from 1946, was intended as a gift for a Mexican politician that Kahlo and her husband knew. Similar to her paintings, Kahlo drew herself with a serious facial expression, like she's asking, “What's my life's meaning?” Also, her eyebrows form the shape of a hummingbird, which seems ready to fly onto her forehead where some cloud-like shapes appear. My favorite part of this drawing is Kahlo’s hair. One side is arranged in a modest braid while the other is loose and wild. I think it shows her inner struggle between two ways of being – reserved versus free.

sections.title: 讲座 2
sections.transcript: 听力原文：(man) During the early twentieth century, technology was advancing rapidly, and music was undergoing a transformation of its own. Electrophones were at the forefront of this evolution. All right, so electrophones. They’re the predecessors of today’s synthesizers. And electrophones challenged established musical conventions. They create sound using electronic means, a groundbreaking innovation for their time. Take for example, the theremin. The theremin is an instrument that let's you create melodies through the manipulation of electromagnetic fields. You don’t even touch it. There’s no direct physical contact with the instrument. The theremin made its mark on the landscape of music, and its tones became synonymous with experimental compositions. Similarly, the ondes Martenot gave musicians a new and expressive range of sounds. You play it by gliding a ring along a wire, kind of like how you move a bow across the strings of a violin. These electrophones, the theremin and the ondes Martenot, set the stage for the synthesizers that dominate today’s music. Electrophones enabled composers of the early twentieth century to explore new musical ideas. Despite being overshadowed by modern electronics, these early electrophones made an important and lasting mark on music, and they continue to influence music-making. Artists are going to keep looking forward in their quest to redefine musical boundaries, but we can also look back to acknowledge the foundational role these early electrophones played in shaping the history of music.

sections.transcript: Imagine a time when the only lights available were flickering candles or oil lamps. Now Fast forward to today, where life is illuminated by the glow of energy efficient LED lights. So what makes these tiny light emitting diodes so revolutionary? Well, the first practical visible spectrum LED was developed in 1962. It was a breakthrough that altered the landscape of lighting technology and set us on a path toward reduced energy consumption. LEDs, that's short for light emitting diodes, are a type of solid-state lighting. They use a semiconductor to convert electricity directly into light. Compared to incandescent bulbs, which waste a lot of energy as heat. LEDs are incredibly efficient. That's their biggest benefit. They use about 75% less energy than incandescent bulbs and last 25 times longer. So that lowers electricity bills and also significantly reduces the carbon footprint. But the impact of LEDs goes beyond energy savings. They've enabled new lighting designs that were previously unimaginable. That's because of their small size, which allows LEDS to be integrated into flexible strips, smart bulbs, and even clothing. So virtually endless possibilities in architecture, art and everyday consumer products. And they're still developing. With ongoing research, we could see such intriguing possibilities as LEDS that can purify the air, improve your mood through human centric lighting, or even transmit data in a system known as Li-Fi, a kind of wireless communication using light from LEDs.

sections.transcript: Listen to part of a history lecture. Listen to part of a history lecture. In the year 1453, the Byzantine Empire ended with the conquest of its capital, Constantinople. After this happened, many Greek scholars who'd lived there fled to Italy, and they brought to Italy their knowledge of ancient Greek language, philosophy, etcetera, which hadn't been preserved particularly well there. Now this knowledge came in the form of manuscripts, which naturally were in ancient Greek. They were written way back before the start of the Byzantine Empire. So the Greek scholars taught Greek to the Italian scholars. They met and worked with Italian translators who translate Greek literature into their own language. This provided new access to ancient Greek knowledge. It led Italian scholars to shift from mainly studying theology to also studying the humanities like history and art. This influence lasted throughout the Renaissance. As you know, the Renaissance is an important period in European history which began in Italy and which saw renewed interest in learning, science and the arts. The city of Venice, Italy, had a large Greek community that grew after 1453 with the influx of Greek scholars. Venice then turned into a hub of classical Greek studies and culture. For one thing, it became a leader in the printing industry and helped spread Greek works in book form. It also became the home of Greek churches and a centre for that religious tradition, which still has a presence throughout Italy.

sections.title: 讲座 2
sections.transcript: By the year 600 CE, writers would make pens out of bird feathers, which they dipped in ink. Interestingly, the technology didn't change a whole lot for over 1,000 years. Then, in the 1930s, a Hungarian newspaper editor named Laszlo Biro was getting frustrated. He had to do a lot of handwriting for his job, but the pens he wrote with would leave smudges. The ink would splatter. Yuck! He also noticed how his newspapers were printed. Newsprint ink didn't smudge, and it dried right away. Now, Laszlo Biro was lucky enough to have a brother who had studied chemistry. They worked together to come up with a ballpoint pen design that could use ink, like what was used on newsprint. Eventually, they came up with a pen that housed a little steel ball in a socket and a small ink barrel that could hold ink paste. It might sound simple, but there was a lot of work involved in figuring out the right size and shape for the components, the composition of the ink, etc. Later, Biro tweaked the pen design not to rely on gravity, so you could hold the pen at different angles and it'd still work. Unfortunately, this was expensive. It wasn't until the 1950s that a French entrepreneur, uh, he improved the design of the ballpoint pen and made it super cheap to make. This is the kind of pen still sold today and which you have most likely seen and used.

sections.title: 讲座 2
sections.transcript: It has a tail, and except for its belly, it's covered in large overlapping scales that make it look kind of like an artichoke or a pine cone. These scales are like its own coat of armor. When it's threatened, the Indian pangolin curls into a tight ball, protecting its belly and using its scales as a shield against predators. This behavior is known as vulvation. Think of a hedgehog. When threatened, a hedgehog will also curl into a ball, vulvation, with its spikes facing outward for protection. Ingenious! The Indian pangolin is found in forests, grasslands, and even deserts. Wherever Indian pangolins are, there's two things they like, digging and ants. Pangolins are nocturnal, meaning they come out at night and when they do they're looking for ants. They eat about two-hundred-thousand of them, ants and termites, every day. This helps keep their ecosystem balanced. They also dig burrows, which are like holes or tunnels to sleep or mate in or to find ants. When Indian pangolins dig, they're disturbing the soil, which improves the soil by making it easier for air, water, and nutrients to circulate in the soil. Similar to why farmers plow their fields, pangolin digging helps contribute to the growth of new, healthy vegetation. Plus, the burrows, once they're abandoned, are good shelter and habitat for other animals.

sections.title: 讲座 2
sections.transcript: (man) Social networks are not just digital online platforms. They're fundamental to understanding how people connect and interact. One powerful tool for analyzing these networks is the sociogram. A sociogram is a visual map that charts relationships within a group. It looks a little like a spider's web. Sociograms illustrate who interacts with whom, how frequently and in what patterns, and by making invisible social structures visible, they reveal dynamics such as influence, isolation, and centrality. Rather than focusing on individual behavior as traditional studies would, sociograms emphasize the web of connections that shape group outcomes. In classrooms, they can identify students who are socially isolated or those who act as bridges between different social groups. In workplaces, social grams help uncover informal hierarchies and where communication breaks down. In public health, they're used to trace contact patterns and predict how diseases might spread from person to person. Sociograms are valuable in marketing as well, where understanding who influences purchasing decisions can guide advertising strategy. However, sociograms do have limitations. By reducing relationships to lines in a web of interactions, they may overlook the subtleties of human interactions, such as trust, conflict, or emotional intensity that aren't easily captured in a diagram. Understanding these qualitative aspects often requires complementary methods like interviews or observation to fully appreciate. Still, when used thoughtfully and alongside other tools, sociograms remain a vital resource for visualizing and analyzing social networks. Their strength lies in turning abstract social dynamics into concrete, interpretable visuals, making them indispensable across disciplines.

sections.title: 讲座 1
sections.transcript: Imagine working in an office where every employee is smiling and enthusiastic. How would it affect your productivity? You'd probably be more productive, but why? See, happy individuals can spread their positive energy, influencing the mood of those around them. This is called emotional contagion. You know when somebody yawns because they're tired or bored, it can make others around them yawn? Well, in this case, instead of yawns, optimism and motivation are spreading. Emotional contagion can happen because of mirror neurons. Mirror neurons fire when you notice someone else's emotion, which makes you feel it too. Importantly, this happens subconsciously. You aren't aware of it or thinking about it when it happens. Now, happiness doesn't just come from perks. Sure, free snacks can help office morale, but real happiness stems from meaningful work, autonomy, and a culture of appreciation. Leadership really sets the tone for that. In turn, happiness enhances creativity, problem solving skills, things like that. So when you're happy, you're not just feeling good, you're thinking better, which motivates you to work better. A study in a leading business magazine takes this further. The authors found that happiness spreads, yes, from a company's leaders to its employees. But what I find remarkable is that the study found that it also extends to the customers or clients. With a positive work environment, the employees feel more committed and engaged. They serve clients better, improving their sense of well-being. And in healthcare settings, that means better health outcomes for clients.

sections.transcript: (man) One tool that's useful in many fields is a Geographical Information System, or GIS. GIS is a computer system that can collect and, uh, store lots of data about specific locations. GIS software can also analyze and display data. You're probably familiar with GPS, which also uses location data. GPS is used for navigation and positioning, and it relies on hardware like satellite, right? Our phones use it. We use GPS on our phones to get directions to places. On the other hand, GIS is software-based and is used for making decisions. Picture a trucking company delivering furniture. They'd use GPS to track where trucks are and where they're headed. The company might use GIS, though, to analyze the amount of fuel that trucks use on particular routes. They'd analyze traffic patterns, elevation changes, things like that, to make decisions about shipping routes. Geographers can use GIS to study the interactions between humans and the environment. Say some farms start using a new fertilizer. GIS can analyze the location of those farms, including nearby streams. GIS can then analyze rainfall patterns in those locations. By combining and analyzing all these data, GIS helps researchers predict where the fertilizer is likely to wind up polluting a stream. Quite useful. GIS software can also create maps of important buildings and sites in historic districts of cities, then assess for things like how development nearby would impact the historic district. This aids with conservation and managing these important locations.
